verse.text: Paul, an apostle—not from people nor through a person, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—
and all the brothers and sisters who are with me, to the assemblies of Galatia:
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address or refer to a mixed group of men and women. Here it refers to fellow believers, and Paul's companions and the Galatian congregations included women. Older translations have 'brethren' or 'brothers'; many recent ones use 'brothers and sisters'.

The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens and, in the Greek Old Testament, Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution, which the word did not mean. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one word.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ,
who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,
to whom be the glory to the ages of the ages. Amen.

note.term: to the ages of the ages

verse.note: The phrase is a Semitic-style idiom meaning 'for all time', and 'for ever and ever' gives its sense accurately. The literal form is kept here because the same word has just been used in verse 4 for 'the present evil age'. Paul sets the present age against the ages to come, and the usual rendering hides that link.

verse.text: I am astonished that you are so quickly turning away from the one who called you in the grace of Christ to a different good news—
verse.note: The Greek noun was an ordinary word for a report of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession, and the related verb means to announce such news. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and remains standard in most translations, but today it suggests a book or a religious term more than an announcement. Using 'good news' and 'proclaim good news' keeps the noun and the verb visibly connected, as they are in the Greek of verses 6–11.

verse.text: not that there is another; it is only that some people are troubling you and want to distort the good news of Christ.
But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should proclaim to you good news contrary to what we proclaimed to you, let him be accursed.
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word translates the Hebrew term for something irrevocably handed over to God, usually for destruction. Paul is not venting anger. He is formally consigning such a person to God's judgment, and he includes himself and angels in the hypothetical.

verse.text: As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone is proclaiming to you good news contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.
For am I now trying to win over people, or God? Or am I seeking to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a slave of Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Many translations soften it to 'servant', partly because of the associations of slavery in modern history. The phrase also echoes the Old Testament title 'slave of the Lord', used of Moses and the prophets, which carried honour as well as total obligation.

verse.text: For I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that the good news proclaimed by me is not of human origin;
for I did not receive it from any person, nor was I taught it, but it came through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek can mean a revelation given by Jesus Christ or a revelation whose content is Jesus Christ. Verse 16, where God reveals his Son, favours the second, though the contrast with 'from any person' fits the first. The English 'of' leaves both possibilities open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism: how I persecuted the assembly of God beyond measure and tried to destroy it,
verse.note: In the New Testament this word occurs only in these two verses. In earlier Jewish writing, notably 2 Maccabees, it names the Jewish way of life as a cause to be zealously defended against outside pressure, and it does not mean a religion set over against 'Christianity'. Paul is describing his former militant devotion to ancestral practice, not a religion he has left for another.

verse.text: and I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, being far more zealous for the traditions of my ancestors.
But when the one who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace was pleased

note.term: the one who set me apart

verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'God, who set me apart'. The edition translated here follows the manuscripts that lack the word 'God', judging it an early clarification by copyists. The meaning is the same either way. The wording echoes the callings of the servant in Isaiah 49:1 and of Jeremiah in Jeremiah 1:5.

verse.text: to reveal his Son in me so that I might proclaim him as good news among the Gentiles, I did not at once consult flesh and blood,
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean 'in me' (an inward revelation), 'to me', or 'through me' (Paul's life as the place where the Son is displayed to others). Many translations choose 'to me'. The same phrase recurs in verse 24, where it is rendered 'because of me'.

The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural it was the regular Jewish term for all peoples other than Israel. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant, but it is a single Greek word throughout.

verse.text: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days;
verse.note: Cephas is the Aramaic name meaning 'rock', of which 'Peter' is the Greek equivalent; the two names refer to the same person. Paul usually uses the Aramaic form. Some later manuscripts substitute 'Peter' here.

verse.text: but I saw none of the other apostles, except James the brother of the Lord.
verse.note: The Greek can be read as counting James among the apostles ('none of the other apostles except James') or as setting him beside them ('none of the other apostles, though I did see James'). The first is the more natural reading and is followed here, but the second is grammatically possible. This James is the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem assembly, not one of the Twelve.

verse.text: As for what I am writing to you—see, before God, I am not lying.
Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
And I was unknown by face to the assemblies of Judea that are in Christ;
they only kept hearing, “The one who once persecuted us is now proclaiming as good news the faith he once tried to destroy,”
and they glorified God because of me.
Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along as well.

I went up in response to a revelation, and I laid before them the good news that I proclaim among the Gentiles—though privately, before those of repute—for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain.
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for the announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so the plain meaning is given. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

The Greek is the plural of the ordinary word for a people or nation; in Jewish usage 'the nations' meant the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders it 'Gentiles' in that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant, but it is one Greek word throughout.

verse.text: But not even Titus, who was with me, though he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised.
But because of the false brothers smuggled in, who slipped in to spy on the freedom we have in Christ Jesus so that they might enslave us—

note.term: because of the false brothers smuggled in

verse.note: Paul's sentence breaks off here and is never grammatically completed; the Greek has no main verb. Some translations supply one ('this matter arose because of...'), making the false brothers the cause of the dispute over Titus; others attach the clause to verse 3 or to verse 5. The translation leaves the break as Paul wrote it.

verse.text: to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the good news might remain with you.
As for those reputed to be something—whatever they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality—those of repute added nothing to me.
verse.note: Literally 'God does not receive a person's face', a Hebrew idiom that entered Greek through the Septuagint. It means favoring someone because of status or appearance. The literal form would not be understood in English, so the sense is given.

verse.text: On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the good news for the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been for the circumcised
(for the one who worked through Peter for an apostleship to the circumcised worked through me also for the Gentiles),

and when they recognized the grace given to me, James and Cephas and John, those reputed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of partnership, so that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.
verse.note: Cephas is the Aramaic form of the name whose Greek equivalent is Peter; both mean 'rock'. Paul uses both forms in this chapter for the same man, and the translation keeps whichever the Greek has in each verse.

The Greek word denotes sharing or joint participation in a common undertaking, and a handshake sealing an agreed division of work suits that sense. 'Fellowship' now suggests friendly association more than a working agreement. Most translations keep 'fellowship'.

verse.text: Only, we were to remember the poor—the very thing I was also eager to do.
But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.
For before certain people came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles; but when they came, he began to draw back and separate himself, fearing those of the circumcision.
verse.note: Literally 'those from circumcision'. The phrase may mean Jewish believers who insisted that Gentile converts be circumcised, or Jews more generally, whether believers or not. It is also unclear whether they are the same people as those who came from James; the translation leaves the phrase open.

verse.text: And the rest of the Jews joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away by their hypocrisy.

But when I saw that they were not walking straight in line with the truth of the good news, I said to Cephas in front of everyone, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?”

note.term: how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts have no quotation marks, and it is disputed where Paul's words to Cephas end. The translation closes the speech here, as most recent versions do. Others carry it through verse 21, and it may be that Paul's report of what he said passes gradually into argument addressed to the Galatians.

verse.text: We are Jews by birth and not sinners from among the Gentiles;

yet, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but only through faith in Jesus Christ, we too believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified.
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: the verb 'justify' here belongs with the noun rendered 'righteousness' in verse 21 and with the adjective 'righteous' or 'just'. To be justified is to be declared or shown to be in the right. Some scholars prefer 'justice' vocabulary throughout to keep the link visible in English.

The Greek is literally 'faith of Jesus Christ'. It can mean either faith in Jesus Christ or the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, that is, his own faithful obedience. The translation follows the traditional and still majority reading, but the other has substantial scholarly support. The same applies to 'faith in Christ' later in the verse.

The phrase means deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses. Scholars dispute whether Paul means law-observance in general or especially the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food rules and the Sabbath. Circumcision and shared meals are the issues in this chapter.

verse.text: But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were also found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
For if I build up again the very things I tore down, I show myself to be a transgressor.
For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ;
it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

note.term: faith in the Son of God
note.traditional: faith in the Son of God

verse.note: As in verse 16, the Greek is literally 'faith of the Son of God'. It may instead mean 'the faithfulness of the Son of God', his own faithfulness shown in giving himself up. The majority reading is followed here; the alternative has substantial scholarly support.

verse.text: I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.
You foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you—you before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly displayed as crucified?
This is the only thing I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?
verse.note: The Greek phrase is compressed: literally 'from hearing of faith'. The first noun can mean the act of hearing or the thing heard (a message or report), and the phrase can be taken as 'hearing accompanied by faith', 'believing what you heard', or 'the message that calls for faith'. The rendering here takes it as the Galatians' own response, set against 'works of the law'; the other readings are widely held.

verse.text: Are you so foolish? Having begun with the Spirit, are you now finishing with the flesh?
Have you suffered so much for nothing—if indeed it was for nothing?
verse.note: The verb almost always means 'suffer' in the New Testament and the Septuagint, and that sense is kept here. In wider Greek it can also be neutral, 'experience', and many interpreters prefer 'Have you experienced so much for nothing?', referring to the Spirit and miracles just mentioned. The letter does not otherwise describe the Galatians' sufferings, so the question remains open.

verse.text: So then, does the one who supplies you with the Spirit and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?
Just as Abraham “believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English uses two: 'righteousness', 'righteous' (verse 11) and 'justify' (verses 8, 11, 24) all share one root, so that to be 'justified' is to be declared or set in the right. Paul's argument in this chapter depends on hearing that connection. Some scholars prefer 'justice' or 'covenant faithfulness' for the noun.

verse.text: Know, then, that those who are of faith, these are the sons of Abraham.
And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced the good news beforehand to Abraham: “In you all the nations will be blessed.”
verse.note: 'Gentiles' and 'nations' in this verse translate the same Greek word, which in the plural means both 'peoples' in general and the non-Jewish peoples in particular. Paul's point rests on that identity: the promise that 'all the nations' would be blessed in Abraham (Genesis 12:3; 18:18) is a promise about the Gentiles.

verse.text: So then, those who are of faith are blessed together with believing Abraham.
For all who are of works of the law are under a curse, for it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.”
And that no one is justified before God by the law is clear, because “The righteous one will live by faith.”

note.term: “The righteous one will live by faith.”
note.traditional: The just shall live by faith

verse.note: The quotation is from Habakkuk 2:4. In Paul's Greek 'by faith' can attach to the verb ('will live by faith') or to the subject ('the one who is righteous by faith will live'). Both readings have strong support; the rendering here follows the word order and leaves the phrase where the Greek puts it.

verse.text: But the law is not of faith; rather, “The one who does them will live by them.”
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree,”
verse.note: The quotation is from Deuteronomy 21:23, which concerns the exposed body of an executed criminal. The Greek word means wood, and so a tree or anything wooden, such as a stake or beam. By Paul's time the text was applied to crucifixion, and the same word is used of the cross elsewhere in the New Testament (for example Acts 5:30).

verse.text: so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
Brothers and sisters, I am speaking in human terms: even a human will, once it has been validated, no one sets aside or adds to.
verse.note: The same Greek word is rendered 'will' here and 'covenant' in verse 17. In everyday Greek it meant a last will and testament; in the Greek Scriptures it was the standard word for God's covenant. Paul announces a human analogy and uses legal vocabulary, so a first-century reader would have heard 'will' here, and Paul then carries the word, and the theme of inheritance, over to God's covenant with Abraham. Many translations keep 'covenant' in both verses; others also have 'will' here.

verse.text: Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say, “And to seeds,” as if speaking of many, but as of one, “And to your seed,” who is Christ.
verse.note: 'Seed' is the ordinary biblical word for descendants, a singular noun normally used collectively, as in the promises to Abraham (Genesis 13:15; 17:8). Paul presses the singular form to say that the promise finds its heir in one person, Christ. In verse 29 he uses the same word collectively for all who belong to Christ. 'Seed' is kept so that the argument from singular and plural can be followed.

verse.text: What I mean is this: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not invalidate a covenant validated beforehand by God, so as to nullify the promise.
For if the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from a promise; but God has given it to Abraham as a gift through a promise.
Why, then, the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.
Now a mediator is not for one party alone, but God is one.

note.term: a mediator is not for one party alone
note.traditional: a mediator is not a mediator of one

verse.note: The Greek says only 'the mediator is not of one, but God is one', and this is among the most disputed sentences in Paul's letters. The usual understanding, followed here, is that a mediator implies more than one party, so the law, given through angels and Moses, is less direct than the promise the one God made in person to Abraham. Other explanations exist, and none has won general agreement.

verse.text: Is the law, then, against the promises of God? Absolutely not! For if a law had been given that was able to give life, then righteousness really would have come from the law.
But the Scripture locked up everything under sin, so that the promise might be given by faith in Jesus Christ to those who believe.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'faith of Jesus Christ', and the grammar allows two readings: faith directed toward Jesus Christ, or the faithfulness of Jesus Christ himself. 'Faith in Christ' is the traditional and still majority reading and is followed here. 'The faithfulness of Jesus Christ' has substantial scholarly support, and on that reading the promise is given on the basis of Christ's own faithfulness to those who believe.

verse.text: Before faith came, we were held in custody under the law, locked up until the faith that was coming would be revealed.
So then, the law became our custodian until Christ came, so that we might be justified by faith.
verse.note: The word names a household slave who had charge of a boy, escorting him to school, supervising his behaviour and disciplining him until he came of age. He was not a teacher, so 'schoolmaster' and 'tutor' mislead, and 'guardian' suggests a legal role he did not have. The image is of temporary supervision and restraint. The phrase 'until Christ' can also be read as 'to lead us to Christ', as older versions have it, but the time references in verses 23 and 25 favour the temporal sense.

verse.text: But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a custodian.
For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God through faith.

note.traditional: children of God / sons of God

verse.note: The word is 'sons' here and in verse 7, and it includes women, as verse 28 makes explicit. Many translations have 'children'. 'Sons' is kept because Paul's argument, continuing into chapter 4, turns on the status of a son as heir and on the believers' share in the standing of God's Son.

In the Greek, 'in Christ Jesus' follows 'through faith', and the traditional rendering joins them: 'through faith in Christ Jesus'. The phrase can equally stand on its own, saying where believers are sons of God, as in 'you are all one in Christ Jesus' in verse 28. The rendering here takes it that way; the traditional reading remains possible.

verse.text: For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to promise.
What I am saying is this: as long as the heir is a minor, he is no different from a slave, though he is master of everything,
but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
So it was with us too: when we were minors, we were enslaved under the elements of the world.

note.traditional: elements of the world; elementary principles of the world; elemental spirits of the world

verse.note: The Greek word meant the basic components of something: letters of the alphabet, the rudiments of a subject, and most often in this period the physical elements (earth, water, air, fire) of which the world was thought to be made. Translations divide between "elementary principles" (basic religious rules) and "elemental spirits" (cosmic powers), though use of the word for spirits is not clearly attested this early. The plain rendering is kept so as not to settle a disputed question. Verses 8–10 connect these elements both with pagan gods and with calendar observance.

verse.text: But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under law,
to redeem those under law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

note.traditional: adoption as sons; the adoption of sons

verse.note: This is the ordinary legal term for adoption, which in the Greco-Roman world usually meant making someone, often an adult male, one's legal heir. "Sons" is kept in verses 5–7 because the argument turns on inheritance and on sharing the status of God's own Son. Paul has just said (3:28) that this status belongs to male and female alike.

verse.text: And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying out, “Abba, Father!”
verse.note: Abba is the Aramaic word for "father", used in addressing one's own father by children and adults alike. Paul gives the Aramaic followed by its Greek equivalent, as in Romans 8:15. Mark 14:36 records Jesus praying with the same double address.

verse.text: So you are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, then also an heir through God.

note.traditional: an heir of God through Christ

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read "an heir of God through Christ", the wording behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses have the shorter and more unusual "through God", which scribes appear to have expanded into more familiar phrasing.

verse.text: But back then, not knowing God, you were slaves to things that by nature are not gods.
Now, though, you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God. How can you turn back again to the weak and impoverished elements? Do you want to be their slaves all over again?
You are observing days and months and seasons and years!
I am afraid for you, that somehow I may have labored over you for nothing.
Become as I am, because I too have become as you are, brothers and sisters; I beg you. You did me no wrong.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to whole congregations. "Brothers" alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are addressed. Several current translations make the same choice.

verse.text: You know that it was because of a bodily illness that I proclaimed the good news to you at first,

note.traditional: infirmity of the flesh; a bodily ailment

verse.note: Literally "a weakness of the flesh". The word commonly means illness and most interpreters take it so here, but it could refer to physical weakness of another kind, such as the effects of injuries. What the condition was is not known. "At first" can also be read as "the first time", which would imply that Paul had visited the Galatians twice.

verse.text: and what was a trial to you in my body you did not scorn or spit at; instead you welcomed me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verse.note: The verb literally means "spit out". Spitting was a familiar gesture both of contempt and of warding off illness or evil, and a first-century reader would probably have heard both. Most translations paraphrase with "reject" or "despise"; the concrete image is kept here.

verse.text: So where is that blessedness of yours now? For I testify to you that, if it had been possible, you would have dug out your eyes and given them to me.
So have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?
They are courting you, but not in a good way; they want to shut you out, so that you will court them.

note.traditional: zealously affect; make much of; are zealous for

verse.note: The verb means to be zealous about someone or to pursue them eagerly, here of rival teachers seeking the Galatians' allegiance. "Court" allows one English word for all three occurrences in verses 17–18, preserving Paul's play on the word. What the Galatians are to be "shut out" from is not stated; most take it to be fellowship with Paul, or full standing among God's people unless they adopt the law.

verse.text: Now it is always good to be courted in a good way, and not only when I am present with you,
my children, with whom I am in labor again until Christ is formed in you.
I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, because I am at a loss about you.
Tell me, you who want to be under law, do you not listen to the law?
For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman.
But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through a promise.
These things are spoken allegorically, for these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery; this is Hagar.
verse.note: The Greek verb can mean either to speak in allegory or to interpret something allegorically. Paul may be saying that the Genesis story itself carries a further meaning, or simply that he is now reading it that way. Scholars disagree, and the rendering leans slightly toward the first.

verse.text: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.

note.term: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
note.traditional: For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia

verse.note: The manuscripts differ here. Some read "For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia", without the name Hagar, and there are other variations. The translation follows the SBLGNT text. Why Paul links Hagar with Sinai is not explained and remains uncertain; on either reading his point is that Hagar belongs with the Sinai covenant.

verse.text: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.

For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who bears no children; break out and shout, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate woman are many, more than those of the woman who has a husband.”
Now you, brothers and sisters, are children of promise, like Isaac.
But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now as well.
verse.note: Genesis 21:9 says only that Sarah saw Hagar's son "playing", and the Greek version adds "with her son Isaac". Some Jewish interpretation understood this as mockery or hostile behaviour, and Paul appears to read the story that way.

verse.text: But what does the scripture say? “Throw out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman will certainly not inherit along with the son of the free woman.”

note.term: “Throw out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman will certainly not inherit along with the son of the free woman.”
note.traditional: Cast out the bondwoman and her son

verse.note: These are Sarah's words to Abraham in Genesis 21:10, which Paul cites as the voice of scripture. He adapts the ending: Genesis has "with my son Isaac", for which Paul writes "with the son of the free woman" to fit his contrast.

verse.text: Therefore, brothers and sisters, we are not children of a slave woman but of the free woman.
For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be held again in a yoke of slavery.

note.traditional: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free

verse.note: The Greek is a bare dative, 'to/for/with freedom'. Most scholars take it as purpose ('for freedom'), but it can also be read as means ('with freedom Christ set us free'). Later manuscripts smooth the wording and join it to the command that follows, which is the form the King James Version translates.

verse.text: Look: I, Paul, tell you that if you have yourselves circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you.
I testify again to every man who has himself circumcised that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
You have been severed from Christ, you who are trying to be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verse.note: 'Justified' here and 'righteousness' in verse 5 translate one Greek word-family, where English has two (just/righteous, justify/righteousness). The verb means to declare or put someone in the right. The present tense describes an attempt in progress, hence 'trying to be justified'.

verse.text: For through the Spirit, by faith, we eagerly await the hope of righteousness.
verse.note: The phrase can mean 'the righteousness we hope for', that is, the final verdict still awaited. It can also mean 'what righteousness leads us to hope for'. Most interpreters prefer the first; the translation keeps the Greek's open wording.

verse.text: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is faith working through love.
You were running well. Who cut in on you and kept you from being persuaded by the truth?
verse.note: The verb means to be persuaded and so to comply, and most translations render it 'obey' here. 'Persuaded' is used to keep Paul's wordplay visible: the same root returns in 'that persuasion' (verse 8) and 'I am persuaded' (verse 10). The sense of yielding to the truth, not merely agreeing with it, is included.

verse.text: That persuasion does not come from the one who calls you.
A little leaven leavens the whole batch of dough.
I am persuaded about you in the Lord that you will think no differently. But the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.
As for me, brothers and sisters, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the stumbling block of the cross has been done away with.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to whole congregations. 'Brothers' alone now sounds male-only in English. Several modern translations render it the same way.

verse.text: I wish those who are unsettling you would go on and castrate themselves!

note.traditional: were even cut off (KJV); emasculate themselves

verse.note: The verb means 'cut off', and in this form it was used of castration. Paul's bitter joke is that those pressing circumcision should let the knife go further. Older English versions softened this to 'cut off', as if he meant exclusion from the community; almost all modern scholars read it as castration.

verse.text: For you were called to freedom, brothers and sisters. Only do not let that freedom become an opening for the flesh, but through love be slaves to one another.
verse.note: From here on, 'flesh' in this chapter is not the physical body as such. It is human nature left to itself, self-directed and opposed to God's Spirit. The list in verses 19–21 shows this, since most of its items (strife, jealousy, factions) are not bodily sins. Some translations paraphrase it as 'sinful nature'; the traditional word is kept because the Greek is the same word used of circumcised flesh earlier in the letter.

The verb is the ordinary word for serving as a slave, from the same root as 'slavery' in verse 1. Most translations soften it to 'serve'. The paradox is deliberate: those freed from the yoke of slavery are to enslave themselves to each other through love.

verse.text: For the whole law is fulfilled in a single saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
What I mean is this: walk by the Spirit, and you will certainly not carry out the desire of the flesh.

note.term: you will certainly not carry out

verse.note: The Greek is an emphatic negative that normally expresses a strong denial about the future, so it is translated here as a promise. A few translations take it as a second command ('and do not gratify'). The grammar favours the promise, and most scholars read it that way.

verse.text: For the flesh desires what is against the Spirit, and the Spirit what is against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do whatever you want.

note.term: so that you do not do whatever you want
note.traditional: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would

verse.note: The clause can express result (the conflict means you do not do what you want) or purpose (each side aims to block what you want). It is also disputed what is frustrated: the good the person wishes to do, the desires of the flesh, or both. The translation leaves this as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under law.
Now the works of the flesh are plain to see: sexual immorality, impurity, debauchery,
idolatry, sorcery, hostilities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of rage, selfish rivalries, dissensions, factions,
envy, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. I tell you in advance, as I told you before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
verse.note: The Greek word covers both 'faith' (trust) and 'faithfulness' (reliability). In a list of qualities shown toward other people, such as patience, kindness and goodness, most modern scholars and translations take it as faithfulness. Older versions have 'faith'.

verse.text: gentleness, self-control. Against such things there is no law.
verse.note: The traditional 'meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a gentle, humble, unassertive manner toward others. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

verse.text: And those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

Brothers and sisters, even if a person is caught in some wrongdoing, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, each of you watching yourself, so that you too are not tempted.
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, as Paul's congregations were. 'Brothers and sisters' says in English what the original hearers understood. Many recent translations do the same, while others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

The verb can mean that the person is discovered by others in the act, or that the person is overtaken by the wrongdoing, taken by surprise by it. 'Caught' leaves both possibilities open. Commentators are divided, and the instruction to restore gently suits either.

Older versions have 'a spirit of meekness'. 'Meek' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not; it describes a considerate, unassertive way of dealing with others. 'Gentleness' is the usual modern rendering.

verse.text: Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.
For if anyone thinks they are something when they are nothing, they are deceiving themselves.
But each person must examine their own work, and then their reason to boast will be in themselves alone and not in someone else,
for each will carry their own load.
verse.note: Verse 2 says to carry one another's burdens and verse 5 that each will carry their own load; the Greek uses two different nouns, and the translation keeps them distinct. The word here was used of a pack or a cargo, and the future tense may point to each person's answerability before God. How sharply the two words differ in meaning is debated, but the two sentences address different situations: mutual help in verse 2, and self-assessment in verses 4–5.

verse.text: The one who is taught the word must share all good things with the one who teaches.

note.traditional: communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things

verse.note: Most interpreters take this as an instruction that those being instructed should support their teachers materially, a practice Paul defends elsewhere. 'Good things' was a common expression for material goods, though some take it more broadly as sharing in everything good.

verse.text: Do not be misled: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that is what they will also reap,
because whoever sows to their own flesh will reap decay from the flesh, but whoever sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.
verse.note: The traditional 'corruption' now suggests bribery or moral dishonesty. The Greek word means rotting, ruin or destruction, which fits the farming image of a crop that spoils and stands in contrast to lasting life.

In Jewish usage this phrase meant the life of the age to come, the life God gives at the final harvest. It describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering and is kept here.

verse.text: Let us not grow tired of doing what is right, for at the proper time we will reap, if we do not give up.
So then, while we have the time, let us do good to everyone, and especially to the members of the household of faith.
See what large letters I am using as I write to you with my own hand.
verse.note: Letters were normally dictated to a secretary, with the sender adding a closing note in his own handwriting. Here Paul takes the pen himself and points out the size of his writing. It may be for emphasis, though other explanations (an unpractised hand, poor eyesight) have been suggested, and none is certain. The Greek refers to the characters, not to the length of the letter as the King James Version suggests.

verse.text: Those who want to make a good showing in the flesh are the ones trying to force you to be circumcised, only so that they will not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.
For not even those who are circumcised keep the law themselves, but they want you to be circumcised so that they can boast in your flesh.
verse.note: The Greek present participle could mean the group pressing circumcision on the Galatians, or people now accepting circumcision under their influence. Most interpreters take it as the former. Some manuscripts have a perfect participle ('those who have been circumcised'), which points more clearly to the former.

verse.text: But as for me, may I never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun can refer either to the cross ('through which') or to Jesus Christ ('through whom'). Both are grammatically possible. Most modern translations choose the cross, since it is the subject of the boasting and the crucifixion language follows immediately.

verse.text: For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything—only a new creation.
And all who walk in line with this rule—peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.

note.term: and upon the Israel of God
note.traditional: and upon the Israel of God

verse.note: This phrase is much disputed. The 'and' may introduce a second group (Jewish people, or Jewish believers in Jesus), or it may be explanatory: 'that is, the Israel of God', describing all who follow this rule, Jew and Gentile alike. The translation keeps the plain 'and', which leaves the question open as the Greek does.

verse.text: From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I carry the marks of Jesus on my body.
verse.note: The Greek word was used for a tattoo or brand that marked a slave, and sometimes a soldier or a devotee of a god, as belonging to a master. Paul most likely means the scars from beatings and stonings suffered in his work, which show whose slave he is. The later idea of 'stigmata' as wounds matching those of the crucifixion is not in view.

verse.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers and sisters. Amen.
